interviewQuestions.question: What problem does QUIC solve that HTTP/2 over TCP couldn't?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd anchor this on transport-layer head-of-line blocking, since that's the specific limitation HTTP/2 hit a ceiling on. HTTP/2 multiplexes many logical requests over one TCP connection, which fixes HOL blocking at the *application* layer — but TCP itself guarantees strictly in-order byte delivery to whatever sits above it. If one TCP segment is lost, TCP withholds every byte after it from the application until that segment is retransmitted and arrives, even bytes belonging to a completely unrelated HTTP/2 stream that never lost anything. Every multiplexed stream on the connection stalls together, and HTTP/2 has no way to fix this from above — the ordering guarantee lives inside TCP itself, a layer HTTP/2 has no visibility into or control over.

QUIC's answer is structural, not a patch: stop using TCP entirely. QUIC runs on top of **UDP** — which imposes no ordering or reliability guarantees of its own — and reimplements reliability, ordering, congestion control, and loss recovery itself, but critically does it **per stream** rather than per connection. A lost packet belonging to stream A only stalls stream A; streams B and C keep flowing uninterrupted, because QUIC tracks and recovers loss independently per stream rather than treating the whole connection as one ordered byte pipe. **HTTP/3** is simply HTTP's existing request/response semantics carried over this new QUIC transport instead of over TCP — the application-level meaning of a GET or a status code doesn't change; what changes underneath it is how bytes get from one side to the other reliably.

The part that shows real depth: this required QUIC to reimplement, in user space, mechanisms (congestion control, retransmission, ordering) that TCP has handled in kernel space for decades — a large undertaking, and why QUIC took years of real-world tuning at Google before IETF standardization.

**Testing:** whether you can name the specific mechanism (TCP's unconditional in-order delivery, decoupled from which stream a byte belongs to) rather than a vague 'QUIC is faster' or 'QUIC uses UDP' without explaining why that matters.

interviewQuestions.question: How does QUIC's handshake compare to TCP + TLS, and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
TCP plus TLS 1.3 needs two sequential round trips before the first application byte can move: one round trip to establish the TCP connection itself (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), and only after that completes, a second round trip to negotiate TLS session keys on top of it. Those round trips are strictly sequential — TLS can't start until TCP is up — so the cost is additive, not overlapping.

QUIC collapses this by design: because QUIC owns both the transport and the crypto handshake as one integrated protocol (TLS 1.3 is built directly into QUIC's handshake, not layered on afterward), it combines connection establishment and key negotiation into a single round trip for a fresh connection — roughly half the setup latency of the TCP+TLS sequence. For a **resuming** client that has connected to this server recently and cached session parameters, QUIC supports **0-RTT**: the client can send actual application data in its very first flight of packets, before any handshake round trip completes at all.

The catch, and the part worth raising unprompted because it shows you understand the trade-off rather than just the win: 0-RTT data is **replayable** by a network attacker who captures and resends those first packets, since there's no fresh randomness yet exchanged to prevent replay. Because of this, 0-RTT is restricted to **idempotent** requests by convention and server policy — a GET is fine to risk replaying, a payment-triggering POST is not — so an application can't blindly rely on 0-RTT for everything; it needs to be aware of which of its requests are safe to send that way.

On a high-latency link — a mobile connection with 100-200ms RTT, or a long-haul international route — shaving even one full round trip off time-to-first-byte is a genuinely felt speedup on real page loads, not just a benchmark number, which is a large part of why QUIC was worth the substantial engineering investment to deploy at scale.

**Testing:** whether you know the concrete round-trip counts for each approach and can articulate the 0-RTT replay trade-off specifically, not just that QUIC's handshake is 'faster.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: QUIC's handshake speed

interviewQuestions.question: What is connection migration in QUIC, and when does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
TCP identifies a connection by a 4-tuple — source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. That's a reasonable design when endpoints are stationary, but it means if your device's IP address changes mid-connection — switching from Wi-Fi to cellular, or roaming between cell towers that reassign your IP — the 4-tuple no longer matches, and from the server's perspective this looks like traffic from an entirely different, unknown connection. The existing TCP connection breaks outright, and the application has to detect the failure and reconnect from scratch, restarting the handshake and, if the application didn't build in its own resume logic, restarting any in-progress transfer too.

QUIC decouples connection identity from the network path entirely by introducing a **connection ID** — a value negotiated at handshake time that both endpoints use to recognize this specific connection, independent of whatever IP and port the packets are currently arriving from. When a client's IP changes, it keeps sending packets tagged with the same connection ID; the server recognizes the connection ID, associates the new source address with the already-established connection state, and traffic continues with no renegotiation and no restarted transfer — QUIC does need to briefly validate the new path isn't spoofed before trusting it fully, but that's a lightweight check, not a fresh handshake.

This matters most concretely for **mobile clients moving between networks mid-session** — a video call that doesn't drop when you leave Wi-Fi range for cellular, a large download that doesn't restart from zero as your train passes between cell towers. These are exactly the scenarios where TCP-based connections visibly hiccup or drop today, and it's a meaningfully better experience for the mobile-heavy traffic patterns that motivated much of QUIC's development.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a specific transport-layer design choice (connection ID vs. 4-tuple identity) to a concrete, felt mobile UX outcome, rather than describing connection migration in the abstract.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Connection migration

interviewQuestions.question: Is QUIC just HTTP/2 running over UDP?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
No, and it's worth correcting this directly and specifically if it comes up, since it's a common but genuinely incorrect mental shortcut. QUIC is not a thin UDP wrapper around HTTP/2's existing framing — it's a substantially redesigned general-purpose transport protocol that HTTP/3 happens to run on top of, and the changes go well beyond swapping the underlying packet type.

Three concrete differences make this clear. First, **loss recovery and congestion control operate per-stream** in QUIC rather than per-connection the way TCP (and by extension HTTP/2 riding on TCP) does — this is the actual mechanism solving transport-layer head-of-line blocking, and it required QUIC to reimplement congestion control algorithms entirely in user space rather than reusing TCP's kernel implementation. Second, QUIC **builds TLS 1.3 into the handshake itself** as an integral part of the protocol, rather than layering encryption on top of an already-established connection the way TCP+TLS does — this is what enables the combined single-round-trip handshake and 0-RTT resumption, neither of which would be possible if crypto were bolted on afterward as a separate step. Third, QUIC introduces **connection migration via connection IDs**, decoupling connection identity from the IP/port 4-tuple entirely — a concept TCP has no equivalent for at all, since TCP's connection identity is inseparable from the network addresses in use.

So the accurate framing is: **HTTP/3** is HTTP's existing request/response semantics carried over QUIC as the transport, analogous to how HTTP/2 carries those same semantics over TCP — but QUIC itself is a from-scratch transport protocol addressing problems TCP structurally can't solve, not a UDP-flavored variant of HTTP/2's framing layer.

**Testing:** that you don't oversimplify QUIC to 'UDP + HTTP/2' — a common but incorrect shorthand — and that you can name the specific structural differences (per-stream recovery, integrated TLS, connection IDs) that make it a genuinely new transport.
